implementation_notes: Ruby's idiomatic mapping is a filter plus a plain object: a before_action :authorize! (or an around_action) in the controller is the Guard, and a plain Ruby class - PostPolicy#update? - is the Policy, obtained by convention from the record; Pundit's authorize @post does exactly that and raises Pundit::NotAuthorizedError when the predicate returns false. Because classes are plain objects and predicates end in ?, the decision is idiomatic without any framework. What replaces the classic structure: the controller filter replaces the Guard class and a one-method policy object replaces the Policy hierarchy; the full pattern with a separate guard object is still justified only when the guard must wrap non-controller entry points (jobs, service objects) uniformly.
idiom_name: before_action filter + plain policy object (Pundit convention)
code_sketch:
class PostPolicy                       # Policy: pure decision
  def initialize(user, post) = (@user, @post = user, post)
  def update? = @user.admin? || @post.author == @user
end

class PostsController < ApplicationController
  before_action :authorize_update!, only: %i[update]     # Guard
  def update = @post.update!(post_params)

  private

  def authorize_update! = authorize @post, :update?      # raises when denied
end
pitfalls: before_action coverage is manual: an action missing from only:/except: is unprotected, so guard the controller (or a base controller) for anything security-relevant.
Rescuing a denial and returning false or nil inside the filter looks safe but hides policy errors; let the denial exception propagate to one rescue_from handler.
Policies that read current_user from a global or thread-local instead of a parameter are hard to test and leak between requests in threaded servers.
